La diaspora philippine au Québec redéfin: The Filipino diaspora in Quebec is redefining resilience by demanding justice, dignity and protections for migrant workers.
Des organisations philippino-canadiennes: Filipino-Canadian organizations, unions and community groups are gathering in Montréal to call for immigration reforms and stronger protections for migrant workers.
<strong>Des associations et des militant: Filipino associations and activists are redefining “resilience” by demanding change in the face of immigration-related precarity, anti-migrant prejudice and the exploitation of migrant workers.
Des groupes de défense philippino-canadi: Filipino-Canadian advocacy groups such as<l1> Migrante</l1> and<l2> PINAY Québec</l2> joined unions and community organizations to mark <l3>International Workers’ Day</l3> on May 1<sup>st</sup>. Earlier, they had organized<l4> demonstrations marking the International Day for the Elimination of Racial Discrimination</l4> in March. Protesters then denounced anti-migrant policies, including Bill C-12, and spoke out against systemic racism, scapegoating and labour exploitation.
« Le discours international sur la “rési: “The international discourse on ‘Filipino resilience’ is often idealized in a way that hides deeper problems. Yes, we are strong and resourceful, but we shouldn’t have to be resilient because systems keep failing us. Sometimes this discourse becomes a way of avoiding talk about accountability, inequality and government neglect,” says France Stohner, founder of<l1> Centre Kapwa</l1> in Montréal, a non-profit organization rooted in restorative justice that aims to decolonize mental health and well-being in the Filipino-Canadian diaspora.
Les récentes manifestations aux Philippi: Recent protests in the Philippines and across the diaspora highlight growing anger over corruption, imperialism and the exploitation of migrants. The “<l1>Trillion Peso March</l1>,” held several times since late 2025, brought tens of thousands of people into the streets to demand accountability for billions of dollars reportedly lost in corruption-plagued flood control projects, and to call for political reform.
Ces derniers mois, la mobilisation s’est: In recent months, the mobilization has continued, leading to<l1> anti-imperialist marches</l1> toward the U.S. Embassy,<l2> demonstrations</l2> denouncing U.S. intervention and war, and<l3> transport strikes</l3> across the country to protest rising fuel prices and economic policies tied to global forces.
<strong>L’histoire de Jean Berly Juan et: Jean Berly Juan’s story and the hidden realities of migrant workers
« Beaucoup d’entre nous sont confrontés: “Many of us face a lack of recognition, precarious working conditions and the constant pressure to provide for our families in the Philippines [...] We often celebrate Filipinos and their strength, but the real struggles and hardships communities go through are not relayed by mainstream media,” says France, pointing to media narratives that overlook lived realities.
L’histoire de Jean Berly Juan est l’une: Jean Berly Juan’s story is one of the many symptomatic experiences lived by the Filipino diaspora in Canada.
Jeune mère monoparentale et ancienne dip: A young single mother and former nursing graduate, Jean Berly made the difficult decision to leave her two-year-old daughter in the Philippines to work as a caregiver in Israel for 10 years and support her family. She arrived in Montréal two years ago through Quebec’s Temporary Foreign Worker Program.
Avec l’aide des recruteurs d’une agence: With the help of recruiters from a Montréal agency, Jean Berly says she was placed in a position with her initial employer that turned out to be coercive. She describes unpaid work, no days off and poor living conditions, as she cared around the clock for her employer’s mother in a retirement home for 10 days. She says her recruiter also falsified documents by filing a tax return for her 2022 income, even though she didn’t arrive in Canada until August 2023.
Alors qu’elle s’installe tranquillement: As she quietly settles into her room, Jean Berly recalls her first days in Montréal with her employer. “She wanted me to live there, at the retirement home, and it was like a hospital. She had given me a bed, but I always felt like I was in a hospital.”
« Dans ce coin, tout le monde peut te vo: “In that corner, everyone can see you. So it wasn’t an environment that suited me. As for food, she would bring me some, but I couldn’t eat what I wanted because I couldn’t cook at the retirement home. And the first thing I wanted was to take a shower, and I couldn’t even do that.”
Jean Berly avait toujours espéré vivre a: Jean Berly had always hoped to live in Canada and bring her family here. Arriving in the country allowed her to realize that dream, but at a considerable price, both personally and financially.
Jean Berly a reçu un jour un diagnostic: Jean Berly was eventually diagnosed with advanced cancer: the disease had spread from her bones to her lungs, then to her brain. The prognosis was dire: one month to live. Today, nearly three years later, she risks falling into a coma if her tumour keeps growing.
« La douleur s’est propagée dans mon dos: “The pain spread to my back; I couldn’t get out of bed anymore. That’s when I went to the hospital, and they told me the cancer was back. When I was in Israel, I had breast cancer [...] At the time, I was recovering.”
« Mais après environ deux mois ici, j’ai: “But after about two months here, I started wondering if something was wrong. Then I noticed tumours starting to appear,” she says, pointing to her collarbone.
Cela fait plus de 7 ans que Jean Bely n’: It has been more than seven years since Jean Berly has seen her daughter, who is now 10. “I really, really want to go home to see my daughter.”
« Parce qu’après toutes ces souffrances: “Because after all this suffering and everything that happened here, she’s the one who gave me the strength to hold on. I hope that when I’m in my own country, I’ll feel better because of my daughter. I don’t think about the six months I have left, I think I’ll have more,” she says, straightening up.
Jean Berly est aujourd’hui aux Philippin: Jean Berly is now in the Philippines with her family: “They give me strength, especially now. It was hard to get used to being away for so long,” she confides.
<strong>Lutter contre la traite des être: Fighting human trafficking and the exploitation of migrants
Depuis 2019, Cheney Cortes travaille com: Since 2019, Cheney Cortes has worked as an immigration advisor at PINAY Québec, which has defended the rights of Filipina migrant women in Quebec since 1991. With the organization’s support, Jean Berly was able to find a new employer and obtained a closed work permit. She left her job, however, after signing an agreement with her employer not to pursue legal action, and without having received her full salary.
Selon Cheney, Jean Berly a investi 8 000: According to Cheney, Jean Berly invested US$8,000 in the migration process, only to be exploited upon arrival. A<l1> Radio-Canada investigation</l1>, in which PINAY and Cheney took part, uncovered hundreds of similar cases, even though the law prohibits charging recruitment fees to low-wage foreign workers.
« De nombreuses agences de recrutement p: “Many unscrupulous recruitment agencies have [...] put many foreign workers into debt; we expect to find many people in precarious situations who have overstayed their authorized period,” says Jasmin de la Calzada, president of PINAY Québec.
Selon Cheney, de nombreux travailleurs s: According to Cheney, many workers end up in vulnerable situations because they pay excessive fees simply to get a job, and they are afraid to report the abuse they experience for fear of losing their work or being expelled from the country.
Beaucoup d’autres, qui se trouvent dans: Many others in similar situations often have no choice but to return to their country of origin because of the obstacles preventing them from obtaining permanent residency. Even applying on humanitarian and compassionate grounds is not a real option.
« Le problème, avec les demandes humanit: “The problem with humanitarian applications is that they take 10 years to process [...] So she won’t get that chance. There is no chance left for her, everything is locked down and she has to go home and die there... it’s literally a suicide,” Cheney continues, discouraged.
Le traitement des demandes pour considér: Processing humanitarian and compassionate applications in Canada takes <l1>two to three years</l1> on average; however, because of a considerable backlog, wait times can reach up to 10 years for some applicants, according to the <l2>current processing times</l2> page.
Maintenant que Jean Berly est aux Philip: Now that Jean Berly is in the Philippines, her initial six-month prognosis no longer matches her situation. According to Cheney, she will no longer be able to afford the treatments she needs. In the Philippines, the health care system is private.
Craignant l’incertitude de son état de s: Fearing the uncertainty of her health and the financial burden it could have placed on her family, Jean Berly chose to return home rather than bring her daughter to Canada, an option that might have allowed her to improve her life expectancy. After many years of separation, she is now reunited with her daughter.
Les travailleurs migrants doivent non se: Migrant workers must not only endure years of family separation, exploitation and the challenges of adapting to a new country, but also face discrimination and prejudice, all while living with the uncertainty created by their immigration status.
« Les travailleurs migrants […] ont été: “Migrant workers […] have been the target of anti-immigrant rhetoric accusing them of being responsible for problems like the housing crisis and the erosion of the French language [...] These racist narratives serve to justify […] restrictive, even violent, immigration policies, like Bill C-12, which is imminent.”
L’<l1>Association canadienne des liberté: The Canadian Civil Liberties Association also expresses serious concerns about Bill C-12, the Strengthening Canada’s Immigration System and Borders Act, in particular the restrictions placed on the fairness of asylum hearings, the government’s discretionary power in processing applications and the possibility of revoking residency documents on vague grounds tied to the “public interest.”
Pendant la pandémie, les règles d’immigr: During the pandemic, immigration rules were relaxed, allowing holders of tourist visas to apply for work permits, which led to a sharp increase in <l1>applications</l1>. In recent years, however, the government has <l2>tightened the rules</l2> by introducing stricter criteria that have led to a large number of refusals.
Les défenseurs des droits affirment que: Rights advocates say these changes have put many migrant workers in precarious situations. When their contracts end, these workers must quickly find a new employer to maintain their status, which has become increasingly difficult because of processing delays.
Le Québec connaît une<l1> pénurie import: Quebec is experiencing a<l1> significant shortage of caregivers and home support workers</l1>, with job openings outnumbering available workers. According to rights advocates, many skilled migrant workers who could help ease this shortfall cannot access these jobs because of restrictions tied to their immigration status.
Les Philippins représentent une part imp: Filipinos make up a significant share of temporary foreign workers and non-permanent residents, particularly in the caregiving and health care sectors. However, since this year, Canada has begun to<l1> reduce the number of work permits granted</l1>, a change that will force many workers to return home.
<strong>Le programme d’exportation de la: The Philippines’ labour export program and its effects on the diaspora
Aujourd’hui, les Philippines continuent: Today, the Philippines continues to rely heavily on exporting its workforce, with about <l1>7,000 Filipinos leaving the country every day</l1>.
Depuis des décennies, les Philippins ont: For decades, Filipinos have been lured by the <l1>idea</l1>, which came from the United States, that working abroad as nurses would ensure their families’ financial security while contributing to the vitality of the economy. In reality, this labour migration helped reduce a critical shortage of health care personnel in the United States and other Western countries. This narrative was thus often explicit and reinforced.
« Je me souviens d’une anecdote racontée: “I remember an anecdote from one of my aunts, who was studying nursing and about to graduate [...] At the next table, there was a sign that said: ‘Nurses wanted in the United States and Canada,’” recalls France, of Centre Kapwa.
« Les Philippines ont une économie qui p: “The Philippines has an economy that pushes its citizens to leave,” France continues. The same dynamic can be seen today in Quebec’s Temporary Foreign Worker Program, which relies on low-cost labour to meet needs while leaving workers in precarious situations.
Jasmin, de PINAY, souligne également que: Jasmin, of PINAY, also points out that Filipino Canadians send more than a billion dollars every year to their loved ones in the Philippines. She finds it particularly heartbreaking to see this hard-earned money undermined by corruption and deteriorating infrastructure, made worse by recurring natural disasters that could have been avoided.
Jess Agustin, défenseur de longue date d: Jess Agustin, a longtime advocate for social justice and migrant rights, points to the lasting effect of American influence in the Philippines:
« En 1945, après la guerre, les États-Un: “In 1945, after the war, the United States gave us so-called independence [...] The Americans had the right to exploit the country and establish permanent military bases there. Marcos stayed in power thanks to U.S. support [...] and he set up this labour export program.”
La dictature de Ferdinand Marcos senior: The dictatorship of Ferdinand Marcos Sr. in the Philippines, from 1965 to 1986,<l1> backed by the United States during the Cold War</l1>, profoundly restructured the Philippine economy [...] by enriching Marcos’s friends and allies, which led to massive debt, widespread poverty and systemic corruption with lasting repercussions for the country’s development.
Le président actuel des Philippines s’ap: The current president of the Philippines is Ferdinand Romualdez Marcos Jr.
<strong>Rassemblement des communautés à: Communities coming together in Montréal and the aspirations of the diaspora
À Montréal en novembre 2025, une collect: In Montréal in November 2025, a fundraiser was held at Buboy in Chinatown after a series of typhoons hit the Philippines. Amid music and surrounded by typically Filipino food and drinks, Shari Ramos, co-founder of<l1> Filipinos of Montreal</l1>, opened up: “The first week after the disaster, nobody had water or electricity [...] The people we’re helping today are actually friends of my cousins [...] It was very hard to deal with, and I’m glad the communities here in Montréal are mobilizing.”
Les crises aux Philippines ne sont pas i: The crises in the Philippines are not isolated. Across borders, communities are demanding that the systems behind displacement, exploitation and inequality be held accountable.
Au Québec, cela se traduit par des appel: In Quebec, this translates into calls for stronger protection against recruitment abuses, better enforcement of laws prohibiting illegal fees, and real accountability for recruitment agencies with questionable practices.
Les défenseurs des droits de la personne: Human rights advocates are also calling for more accessible pathways to permanent residency, fair immigration processes and an end to policies that keep migrant workers in precarious and vulnerable situations.
« Les Philippins du Québec et du Canada: “Filipinos in Quebec and Canada show resilience in their resistance to corruption, both in the Philippines and in their host countries [...] They aren’t sitting idly by, but are expressing their anger and outrage in the streets,” says Jasmin, of PINAY.
« Ce qui alimente notre militantisme, c’: “What fuels our activism is hope,” says Jess Agustin. “Hope for a country we still love [...] You see our despair at the lack of change, and then you look and see young people mobilizing [...] making the connection: the effects of American imperialism, of colonialism [...] You have a culture that is quite damaged, but you also see young people reviving Indigenous culture and developing the vision of a society [where] they no longer have to leave the country.”
Au Québec, des groupes philippins contes: In Quebec, Filipino Groups Challenge Migration Policies and Workplace Abuse
Des groupes philippino-canadiens dénonce: Filipino-Canadian groups are denouncing the exploitation of migrant workers, racism and restrictive immigration policies, saying that “Filipino resilience” must not mask systemic inequalities. Through Jean Berly Juan’s testimony and the mobilization of organizations like PINAY Québec, the diaspora is calling for stronger protections, pathways to permanent residency and greater accountability for employers and recruiters.
